newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr creeps off lows, but recovery eludes.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr creeps off lows, but recovery eludes.

text.p: The Australian dollar crept higher at the midsession as early support prompted scattered short-covering but shied away from testing US$0.7770 resistance.
Dealers said activity was light as most major players were concentrating on selling the U.S. dollar against a revived mark and had little interest in a range-bound Aussie.

Investors were also made cautious by expectations of offshore demand linked to the sale of a Victorian power station, the final details of which could come at any time, and by fears the verdict on a national minimum wage claim, due Tuesday, would be benign enough to stoke speculation of another rate cut.
By 12.30 pm (0230 GMT) the local dollar had drifted up to US$0.7756/61 from an offshore low around US$0.7725 and even added a bit to Friday's late US$0.7750/55.
Resistance at US$0.7770 had proved formidable last week, however, and dealers said offers were still thought to be crowded there, effectively capping the currency for now.

Equally, support had been solid around US$0.7720 and sellers were reluctant to test it while the threat of the power station deal lay in the wings. Rumour put the selling price at around A$4.5 billion, implying the offshore-led group that won the bidding would have some need to buy Australian dollars.

Dealers emphasised the actual amount of direct A$ demand was hard to gauge -- it would certainly be less than the total selling price -- as was the timing of payments by the bidder. But the possibility alone should tend to support the dollar until the details were known.
The support might be needed if Tuesday's award on the "living wage" claim proved as modest as some were predicting.

The main Australian trade union body had asked for an 8.75 percent increase in award wages and three A$20 per week pay rises over three years for workers who failed to win enterprise agreement increases.
The claim was attacked by the government and the Reserve Bank, with the latter estimating it could add more than 1.6 percent points to national wages growth and boost unemployment.
The RBA even warned that granting the full claim could ultimately force it to tighten policy to protect its 2-3 percent target for underlying inflation.

Analysts believe the threat would have told with the Industrial Relations Commission, an independent body which rules on such claims, and it would only grant a weekly rise of A$10 to A$15. Such a result might not only eclipse all thought of a hike but even stoke speculation the central bank could cut again.

Talk of a cut has been building since March jobs figures showed a second monthly fall in employment and a steady drip of other data suggested the economy was slow to respond to the three easings delivered last year.
Apart from the concern over wages, inflation was not a worry as first quarter consumer price data on Wednesday were expected to confirm.

The annual underlying rate was seen staying at 2.1 percent, the very bottom of the RBA's 2-3 percent target rate, while headline inflation should slow to a four-year low of 1.2 percent. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
